content:
BUILDING A CI/CD PIPELINE ON AWS: INTEGRATING DEVSECOPS TO PERFORM SECURITY CHECKS BEFORE PRODUCTION DEPLOYMENT In modern software development, deploying source code to a Production environment quickly is no longer enough. An application may function normally while still containing security vulnerabilities, unsafe third-party dependencies, or AWS configurations that have not been properly secured.
If security checks are only performed after an application has been deployed, identifying and fixing issues can take more time, increase costs, and potentially affect system operations.
An effective solution is to integrate DevSecOps into the CI/CD Pipeline on AWS. This approach incorporates security checks throughout the development and deployment process, helping teams identify potential risks before the application is released to the Production environment.
Architecture Overview The CI/CD architecture integrated with DevSecOps uses multiple AWS services to automate application building, security testing, deployment, and system monitoring.
The main components include:
Git: Manages source code and tracks changes made by developers. AWS CodePipeline: Orchestrates the entire CI/CD workflow. AWS CodeCommit: Stores the repository containing the application’s source code. AWS CodeBuild: Builds the application and performs security checks. AWS CodeDeploy: Deploys the application to the target environment. Amazon S3 & AWS CodeArtifact: Store build artifacts and dependencies required during the build and deployment processes. AWS Lambda: Analyzes security scan results and supports the handling of security findings. AWS Security Hub: Aggregates security findings from multiple sources. AWS Config: Monitors and evaluates the configurations of AWS resources. Amazon ECS: Runs the application in Staging and Production environments. CI/CD Process Integrated with DevSecOps The workflow is divided into several stages to ensure that the application is properly checked before being released to the Production environment.
1. Commit – Push Source Code to Git
When developers complete a source code change, they commit and push the changes to the repository.
Git records changes made to the source code. AWS CodePipeline receives an event from the repository to trigger the pipeline. The build and testing stages are executed automatically. 2. Build & Security Scan – Source Code Inspection
AWS CodeBuild builds the application and integrates security testing tools into the workflow.
Two important security testing methods include:
SCA (Software Composition Analysis): Checks third-party libraries and dependencies used by the application. Identifies dependency versions with known security vulnerabilities or potential risks. SAST (Static Application Security Testing): Analyzes source code without executing the application. Detects code patterns or programming practices that may introduce security weaknesses. In the illustrated architecture, the tools used include Black Duck and SonarQube.
3. Deploy – Deployment to the Staging Environment
After the initial build and security checks are completed, the application is deployed to the Staging environment.
AWS CodeDeploy manages the deployment process. Amazon ECS provides the environment in which the application runs. Staging acts as a testing environment before the application is released to Production. 4. Test – Security Testing During Application Runtime
After deployment to Staging, the system continues performing security checks while the application is running.
DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing): Tests a running application by sending requests and analyzing the responses. Identifies vulnerabilities that may appear during application execution. IAST (Interactive Application Security Testing): Analyzes application behavior during runtime. Helps detect security issues based on information collected while the application is operating. In the illustrated architecture, the tools used include Appknox and Veracode.
5. Manual Approval & Production Deployment
Before the application is officially released, the testing results must be collected and evaluated.
Review identified security issues and warnings. Assess risk levels and determine which issues need to be fixed. Require Manual Approval before proceeding with Production deployment. If the application meets the necessary requirements, AWS CodeDeploy deploys it to Amazon ECS in the Production environment. Adding a manual approval stage helps development and security teams maintain better control over the application release process.
Security Monitoring and Control In addition to source code and application testing, the system needs monitoring mechanisms to track activities and detect unusual changes.
Several AWS services support this process:
AWS CloudTrail: Records API activities and changes made within the AWS account. AWS Config: Monitors resource configurations and identifies changes that do not comply with established requirements. AWS Security Hub: Aggregates security findings from multiple services to support risk assessment. AWS Lambda: Analyzes scan results and helps automate the handling of certain security findings. Amazon CloudWatch Logs & Events: Monitors logs, events, and the execution status of the pipeline. Combining these services gives DevOps and Security teams a more comprehensive view of the system’s security status.
Configuration and Access Management A secure CI/CD Pipeline requires more than source code inspection. It must also control access permissions and protect application configuration information.
Important components include:
AWS IAM Role: Grants AWS services the permissions required to perform their tasks. Applies the Least Privilege principle by granting only the permissions that are actually necessary. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store: Stores and manages application configuration parameters. Reduces the need to place configuration information directly in source code. Amazon S3: Stores artifacts required during the build and deployment processes. Amazon SNS (Simple Notification Service): Sends Email notifications when pipeline activities or security checks generate events that require attention. Scenarios to Validate To ensure that the pipeline works as expected, several practical scenarios should be tested:
Vulnerable Dependencies: SCA detects an unsafe library and generates a warning before deployment. Source Code Security Issues: SAST identifies potential security problems during the build stage. Runtime Application Vulnerabilities: DAST and IAST help detect issues in the Staging environment. Insecure AWS Configurations: AWS Config records resources that do not meet the required configuration standards. Deployment Failure: CloudWatch Logs helps monitor and identify the causes of deployment errors. Security Risk Detection: Security Hub aggregates findings so that DevOps and Security teams can review and resolve them. These scenarios help evaluate the pipeline’s ability to detect, report, and control security risks throughout its operation.
What I Learned Through this CI/CD architecture integrated with DevSecOps, I gained a better understanding that security should be considered an essential part of the software development process rather than simply a final check before release.
Some important lessons include:
Integrating SCA and SAST into the build stage to detect dependency and source code issues early. Using DAST and IAST to test applications in a running environment. Deploying applications to Staging before releasing them to Production. Adding Manual Approval to control important changes before release. Combining Security Hub, AWS Config, and CloudTrail to improve security monitoring and control. Applying the IAM Least Privilege principle to limit unnecessary access permissions. The most important lesson I learned is that DevSecOps changes the security approach from checking applications only after deployment to performing continuous security checks throughout the software development lifecycle.
As a result, organizations can identify vulnerabilities earlier, reduce potential risks, and improve application reliability before releasing software to the Production environment.

title: Week 5 Worklog
content:
Objectives for Week 5 Gain a general understanding of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) and its role in modern applications. Understand the fundamental concepts of Large Language Models (LLMs), Foundation Models, and methods for applying language models. Explore Amazon Bedrock and its capabilities for developing Generative AI applications on Amazon Web Services (AWS). Study Prompt Engineering and techniques for improving the quality of AI-generated responses. Research Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Embeddings, Vector Databases, and Knowledge Bases. Understand AI Agent architectures and how AI models can be integrated with APIs, tools, and external data sources. Tasks to Be Completed This Week Day Tasks Start Date Completion Date References Monday - Explore Generative AI and its real-world applications. - Study Large Language Models (LLMs) and Foundation Models. - Understand the differences between Traditional AI, Generative AI, and Agentic AI. - Research AI applications in software development, natural language processing, and automation. 19/10/2026 19/10/2026 AWS Generative AI Tuesday - Explore Amazon Bedrock and its main capabilities. - Study how Amazon Bedrock provides access to Foundation Models. - Learn about Model Inference, Tokens, Context Windows, and Model Parameters. - Research Prompt Engineering and different prompting techniques. - Explore methods for testing and evaluating AI-generated responses. 20/10/2026 20/10/2026 Amazon Bedrock Prompt Engineering Wednesday - Study Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and its role in Generative AI applications. - Research Embeddings and Vector Databases. - Explore Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. - Study document collection, chunking, information retrieval, and response generation. - Analyze the advantages and limitations of RAG-based systems. 21/10/2026 21/10/2026 Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases Thursday - Understand AI Agents and Agentic AI. - Explore AI Agent architectures, including LLMs, Tools, Memory, and APIs. - Study Amazon Bedrock Agents and how their components work together. - Research the integration of AI Agents with AWS Lambda and Backend services. - Explore real-world applications of AI Agents. 22/10/2026 22/10/2026 Amazon Bedrock Agents Friday - Review Generative AI, Amazon Bedrock, RAG, and AI Agents studied throughout the week. - Compare Generative AI and Agentic AI in terms of operating principles and practical applications. - Research methods for evaluating the quality of language model responses. - Explore challenges in deploying Generative AI applications, including accuracy, latency, security, and cost. - Complete technical notes on Generative AI technologies available on AWS. 23/10/2026 23/10/2026 AWS Generative AI AWS Documentation Expected Achievements for Week 5 1. General Knowledge of Generative AI Understand the concept of Generative AI and its role in content generation, information processing, and task automation.
Differentiate between important AI concepts:
Traditional AI: AI systems designed to perform tasks such as classification, prediction, and recognition.
Generative AI: AI technology capable of generating new content, including text, images, software code, and other forms of data.
Agentic AI: An approach to developing AI systems capable of using tools and coordinating multiple processing steps to accomplish tasks.
Explore common applications of Generative AI:
Chatbots and Virtual Assistants. Document Summarization and Text Analysis. Software Development and Coding Assistance. Information Retrieval and Processing. Workflow Automation. 2. Knowledge of Large Language Models and Foundation Models Understand Large Language Models (LLMs) and their capabilities in processing, analyzing, and generating natural language.
Learn fundamental concepts:
Foundation Model: A model trained on large amounts of data that can be adapted to different tasks.
Large Language Model (LLM): A large-scale language model capable of processing and generating text.
Token: A unit of data used by a model when processing input and generating output.
Context Window: The maximum amount of context a model can process within a single interaction.
Inference: The process of using a trained model to generate predictions or responses.
Understand the role of LLMs in Generative AI applications and AI Agents.
3. Knowledge of Amazon Bedrock Understand Amazon Bedrock as a managed AWS service that supports the development and scaling of Generative AI applications.
Explore how Amazon Bedrock provides access to various Foundation Models through supported interfaces and APIs.
Study important components and capabilities:
Foundation Models: AI models designed for tasks such as text generation, data analysis, and content processing.
Model Inference: The process of sending input data to a model and receiving a generated result.
Knowledge Bases: Support the integration of AI models with external data sources and knowledge repositories.
Agents: Support the development of AI systems capable of performing tasks and interacting with external tools.
Recognize the importance of selecting suitable models based on output quality, response time, task compatibility, and cost.
4. Knowledge of Prompt Engineering Understand the role of Prompt Engineering in improving the quality of responses generated by language models.
Study common prompting techniques:
Zero-shot Prompting: Asking a model to perform a task without providing examples.
Few-shot Prompting: Providing several examples to guide the model in performing a task.
Role-based Prompting: Defining a specific role or context for the model.
Structured Prompting: Designing prompts with clearly defined tasks, input information, and expected output formats.
Recognize the importance of testing and evaluating model responses instead of relying on a single generated result.
5. Knowledge of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Understand Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) as an approach that combines information retrieval from external data sources with the response-generation capabilities of language models.
Study the fundamental components of a RAG system:
Document Processing: Preparing and processing source documents.
Chunking: Dividing documents into smaller sections suitable for retrieval.
Embeddings: Representing data as numerical vectors.
Vector Database: A system that stores and searches vectors based on similarity.
Retriever: A component responsible for finding information relevant to a user’s query.
LLM: A language model that uses retrieved information to generate a response.
Study the basic RAG workflow:
Collect and prepare source data. Divide documents into smaller chunks. Convert document content into embeddings. Store data for efficient retrieval. Receive a question from the user. Retrieve relevant information. Provide retrieved context to the language model. Generate a response based on the question and retrieved information. Understand the advantages and limitations of RAG, particularly its dependence on data quality and retrieval performance.
6. Knowledge of AI Agents and Agentic AI Understand the concept of AI Agents and their ability to perform tasks through the use of external tools.
Explore the common components of an AI Agent architecture:
LLM: Supports request interpretation, reasoning, and response generation.
Tools: External capabilities that an AI system is authorized to use when performing tasks.
Memory: Mechanisms for maintaining information or context when required by an application.
API Integration: Enables AI systems to communicate with external services and data sources.
Workflow: Defines how different components coordinate to accomplish a task.
Study Amazon Bedrock Agents and related components, including Foundation Models, Instructions, Action Groups, and Knowledge Bases.
Explore the integration of AI Agents with AWS services and Backend applications.
Recognize the importance of access control, output evaluation, and activity monitoring when developing AI Agent systems.
7. Comparison Between Generative AI and Agentic AI Criteria Generative AI Agentic AI Primary Objective Generate content or responses based on input Perform tasks through multiple processing steps Tool Integration Depends on application design Commonly integrates tools and APIs to execute tasks Operating Mechanism Processes requests and generates outputs May plan, select tools, and coordinate multiple actions Common Applications Chatbots, content generation, text summarization Automation assistants, workflow processing, system integration Challenges Accuracy, output quality Action control, security, reliability, and cost Through this comparison, I aim to gain a clearer understanding of the differences between traditional Generative AI applications and Agentic AI systems that coordinate multiple tools to accomplish tasks.
8. Knowledge of Generative AI Evaluation and Deployment Explore important factors when evaluating Generative AI applications:
Response Quality: The relevance and usefulness of generated responses.
Accuracy: The correctness of information produced by the AI model.
Latency: The time required to process a request and return a response.
Cost: Expenses associated with model usage and supporting services.
Security: The protection of sensitive data and control of access permissions.
Reliability: The ability to maintain stable and consistent system operation.
Study Hallucination, a phenomenon in which AI models generate inaccurate or unsupported information.
Recognize the importance of testing, response evaluation, and monitoring during AI application development.
Understand the importance of selecting suitable models, designing effective prompts, and organizing appropriate data sources to improve system quality.
9. Week 5 Summary The fifth week of the internship focuses on exploring Generative AI technologies and their applications on Amazon Web Services.
The main topics include Large Language Models, Foundation Models, Amazon Bedrock, Prompt Engineering, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and AI Agents.
Through studying these technologies, the objective is to understand how artificial intelligence models can be integrated with data sources, APIs, and external tools to develop intelligent applications.
Additionally, researching techniques such as Prompt Engineering and RAG helps expand knowledge of methods for improving the quality of language model responses.
Exploring Agentic AI also provides a better understanding of how AI systems can coordinate multiple components to perform complex tasks.
Beyond technical knowledge, the week also covers important factors in evaluating and deploying Generative AI applications, including accuracy, response time, security, reliability, and cost.
These topics provide foundational knowledge of Generative AI and AI services on AWS while expanding an understanding of emerging trends in modern artificial intelligence applications.

title: Worklog
Week 4 Worklog
content:
Objectives for Week 4 Understand the fundamentals of Serverless Computing and its role in application development on Amazon Web Services (AWS). Gain foundational knowledge of AWS Lambda and how it enables developers to run code without directly managing servers. Explore important AWS Lambda components, including Functions, Runtimes, Triggers, Events, and Execution Roles. Understand Amazon API Gateway and how APIs enable communication between client applications and backend services. Study Amazon CloudWatch for application monitoring, log collection, and performance analysis. Explore how AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) controls access permissions between AWS services. Become familiar with the process of designing, deploying, and testing a basic Serverless application. Build foundational knowledge of application deployment to support the development of the final internship project. Tasks to Be Completed This Week Day Tasks Start Date Completion Date References Monday - Study the fundamentals of Serverless Computing and the characteristics of serverless architectures. - Compare Serverless Computing with traditional application deployment models. - Explore AWS Lambda and its common use cases. - Understand Functions, Runtimes, Events, and Triggers. 12/10/2026 12/10/2026 AWS Lambda Documentation Tuesday - Study the architecture and execution process of AWS Lambda. - Learn about Lambda Execution Roles and AWS IAM permissions. - Explore event processing and function invocation in AWS Lambda. - Study how to create and test Lambda Functions using Python. - Practice with an authorized AWS environment if available. 13/10/2026 13/10/2026 AWS Lambda Developer Guide Wednesday - Explore Amazon API Gateway and the role of APIs in software systems. - Study REST APIs, HTTP Methods, and HTTP Status Codes. - Understand how API Gateway integrates with AWS Lambda. - Learn how HTTP Requests are processed and HTTP Responses are returned. - Explore the design of a simple Serverless REST API. 14/10/2026 14/10/2026 Amazon API Gateway Documentation Thursday - Study Amazon CloudWatch and its application monitoring capabilities. - Explore CloudWatch Logs, Metrics, and Alarms. - Learn how to monitor Lambda execution duration, invocations, and errors. - Understand how CloudWatch Logs support debugging and troubleshooting. - Research security and cost management principles for Serverless applications. 15/10/2026 15/10/2026 Amazon CloudWatch Documentation Friday - Review AWS Lambda, API Gateway, and CloudWatch. - Design a basic Serverless application architecture diagram. - Explore the integration process between Lambda and API Gateway. - Develop or simulate a simple API to examine HTTP Request and Response processing. - Summarize Week 4 and prepare to study Generative AI on AWS in Week 5. 16/10/2026 16/10/2026 AWS Serverless AWS Workshops Achievements in Week 4 1. General Knowledge of Serverless Computing Developed an understanding of Serverless Computing and its role in modern application development.
Learned that Serverless Computing enables developers to focus on application code without directly managing the underlying server infrastructure.
Explored the main characteristics of serverless architectures:
Automatic Scaling: Computing resources can automatically adapt to changing application workloads. Event-Driven Architecture: Functions can be invoked in response to specific events. Managed Infrastructure: The cloud provider manages many infrastructure components. Pay-per-use: Pricing depends on the resource consumption and billing model of each service. Understood the differences between serverless architectures and traditional application deployment models.
Identified common serverless use cases, including API processing, data processing, and workflow automation.
2. Knowledge of AWS Lambda Understood AWS Lambda as a serverless computing service that executes code in response to events.
Learned about the fundamental components of AWS Lambda:
Lambda Function: A unit of application code deployed and executed through AWS Lambda. Runtime: The execution environment supporting compatible programming languages and versions. Event: Input data provided when a Lambda Function is invoked. Trigger: A component or service that initiates function execution. Execution Role: An IAM Role granting a Lambda Function the permissions required to access AWS resources. Studied the basic AWS Lambda execution process:
An event or request invokes a Lambda Function. AWS Lambda receives the request and prepares an execution environment when necessary. The function processes input data using the deployed application code. The processing result is returned or delivered to another component. Execution information may be recorded for monitoring and troubleshooting. Recognized the role of AWS Lambda in developing backend services for modern applications.
Became familiar with the structure of a Python-based Lambda Function.
3. Knowledge of Amazon API Gateway Learned that Amazon API Gateway is a managed service for creating, publishing, maintaining, monitoring, and securing APIs.
Understood the role of API Gateway in connecting client applications with backend services.
Studied fundamental API concepts:
REST API: An API based on REST architectural principles, commonly using HTTP for communication. API Endpoint: A URL through which clients can access an API. HTTP Request: A message sent by a client to request an operation or resource. HTTP Response: A message returned after processing a request. HTTP Methods: Common methods such as GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE. HTTP Status Codes: Response codes indicating request outcomes, such as 200, 400, 404, and 500. Explored the integration between Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda.
Understood how API Gateway receives HTTP requests and invokes Lambda Functions to process them.
Studied the process of developing simple APIs for web and mobile applications.
4. Knowledge of Amazon CloudWatch Understood Amazon CloudWatch and its role in monitoring AWS applications, resources, and services.
Explored its major components:
CloudWatch Logs: Collects, stores, and supports the analysis of application and service logs. CloudWatch Metrics: Provides measurements for monitoring system activity and performance. CloudWatch Alarms: Monitors metrics and performs configured actions when alarm conditions are met. CloudWatch Dashboards: Provides visual representations of monitoring data. Studied important AWS Lambda metrics:
Invocations: The number of times a Lambda Function is invoked. Duration: The time taken to execute a function. Errors: The number of function invocations that result in errors. Throttles: The number of invocation requests rejected due to concurrency or other execution limits. Understood how CloudWatch supports issue detection, performance monitoring, and application troubleshooting.
5. Knowledge of IAM and Serverless Security Explored the role of AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) in controlling access permissions between AWS services.
Understood how Lambda Execution Roles determine which AWS resources a function can access.
Studied the Principle of Least Privilege when assigning permissions to serverless applications.
Recognized the importance of:
Granting functions only the permissions necessary to perform their tasks. Protecting credentials and sensitive information. Controlling access to APIs. Monitoring application activities through logs. Tracking resource consumption and service costs. 6. Understanding the Serverless Application Development Process Studied a basic serverless architecture involving Amazon API Gateway, AWS Lambda, and Amazon CloudWatch.
Understood the application request-processing workflow:
A client sends an HTTP Request to an API Endpoint. Amazon API Gateway receives and routes the request. API Gateway invokes the integrated Lambda Function. The Lambda Function processes the request data. The processing result is returned to API Gateway. API Gateway sends an HTTP Response to the client. Execution information is recorded by monitoring services when logging is appropriately configured. Identified the components required to develop a simple REST API.
Became familiar with API testing using HTTP request tools.
Recognized the importance of result validation, error handling, and log monitoring during application development.
7. Comparison of AWS Serverless and Monitoring Services Service Main Function Role in an Application AWS Lambda Serverless code execution Processes backend application logic Amazon API Gateway API creation and management Receives and routes client requests Amazon CloudWatch Application and resource monitoring Collects metrics, logs, and alerts AWS IAM Identity and access management Controls permissions between AWS services and resources Through studying these services, I developed a clearer understanding of how different AWS components work together to create backend applications without directly managing servers.
8. Week 4 Summary During the fourth week of my internship, the main focus was on Serverless Computing and AWS services used to develop, deploy, and monitor cloud-based applications.
By studying AWS Lambda, I gained a better understanding of event-driven code execution and the benefits of managed computing services.
Exploring Amazon API Gateway helped me understand how client applications communicate with backend services through HTTP-based APIs.
In addition, studying Amazon CloudWatch and AWS IAM highlighted the importance of monitoring, troubleshooting, security, and access management in cloud application development.
Beyond theoretical knowledge, exploring the integration between API Gateway and Lambda provided a clearer understanding of the process of designing, developing, and testing a basic Serverless application.
The knowledge acquired during Week 4 will provide a foundation for studying Generative AI, Large Language Models (LLMs), AI Agents, and Amazon Bedrock in Week 5, while preparing for the research and development phase of my final internship project.

title: Week 3 Worklog
content:
Objectives for Week 3 Gain an overview of data storage and management methods on Amazon Web Services (AWS). Understand the differences between three common storage models: Object Storage, Block Storage, and File Storage. Explore AWS storage services, including Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS), and Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS). Understand the fundamentals of relational databases and non-relational (NoSQL) databases. Study Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) and Amazon DynamoDB. Explore data protection, access control, and backup methods on AWS. Become familiar with data management through the AWS Management Console. Build foundational knowledge of Storage and Database services to support Cloud and AI applications in the following weeks. Tasks to Be Completed This Week Day Tasks Start Date Completion Date References Monday - Explore Storage in Cloud Computing. - Differentiate between Object Storage, Block Storage, and File Storage. - Study Amazon S3 and the concepts of Buckets, Objects, Keys, and Storage Classes. - Explore real-world use cases of Amazon S3. 05/10/2026 05/10/2026 Amazon S3 Documentation Tuesday - Study Amazon S3 features. - Explore S3 Versioning, Lifecycle Rules, and Bucket Policies. - Research access management and data protection methods in Amazon S3. - Learn how to create S3 Buckets and upload, download, and manage Objects. - Practice basic S3 operations if an authorized AWS environment is available. 06/10/2026 06/10/2026 Amazon S3 User Guide Wednesday - Study Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS) and its role in Amazon EC2. - Explore EBS Volumes, Snapshots, and commonly used EBS Volume types. - Learn about Amazon Elastic File System (EFS). - Compare Amazon S3, EBS, and EFS in terms of storage methods, capabilities, and use cases. 07/10/2026 07/10/2026 Amazon EBS Amazon EFS Thursday - Explore Database services in Cloud Computing. - Differentiate between Relational Databases and NoSQL Databases. - Study Amazon RDS, supported database engines, and basic management features. - Explore Amazon DynamoDB and the NoSQL data model. - Compare Amazon RDS and DynamoDB in terms of data structure, scalability, and use cases. 08/10/2026 08/10/2026 Amazon RDS Amazon DynamoDB Friday - Review AWS Storage and Database services studied during the week. - Explore data backup and recovery methods, including S3 Versioning, EBS Snapshots, and RDS Backups. - Study data security principles and access management. - Create a comparison table of Amazon S3, EBS, EFS, RDS, and DynamoDB. - Summarize Week 3 and prepare to study AWS Serverless services in Week 4. 09/10/2026 09/10/2026 AWS Documentation Achievements in Week 3 1. General Knowledge of Cloud Storage Developed an understanding of the role of storage services in managing and processing data in cloud computing environments.
Learned to distinguish between three fundamental storage models:
Object Storage: Stores data as objects and is suitable for images, videos, documents, unstructured data, and applications requiring scalability.
Block Storage: Stores data in blocks and is commonly used as disk storage for servers and systems requiring block-level access.
File Storage: Organizes data into files and directories, supporting data access and sharing across multiple systems.
Understood the fundamental characteristics of each storage model and their appropriate use cases.
2. Knowledge of Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) Understood the concept of Amazon S3 and its role as an object storage service.
Explored the fundamental components of Amazon S3:
Bucket: A container used to store objects.
Object: The fundamental unit of data stored in Amazon S3.
Object Key: A unique identifier for an object within a bucket.
Storage Class: A storage option designed for specific data access patterns and cost requirements.
Studied important Amazon S3 features:
S3 Versioning: Maintains multiple versions of objects to support data recovery and management.
S3 Lifecycle Rules: Automatically transitions or expires objects based on configured rules.
Bucket Policies: Define access permissions for resources stored in S3 buckets.
S3 Encryption: Protects stored data using encryption mechanisms.
Understood the basic process of creating buckets, uploading and downloading files, and managing objects through the AWS Management Console.
Recognized the importance of configuring appropriate access permissions and preventing unnecessary public access to stored data.
3. Knowledge of Amazon EBS and Amazon EFS Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS)
Learned that Amazon EBS provides block storage commonly used with Amazon EC2.
Understood the following concepts:
EBS Volume: A block-level storage device that can be attached to a compatible EC2 instance.
EBS Snapshot: A backup of an EBS volume that supports data protection and recovery.
Volume Types: Different storage options optimized for specific performance and cost requirements.
Understood the role of EBS in providing persistent storage for applications running on EC2 instances.
Amazon Elastic File System (EFS)
Understood Amazon EFS as a managed file storage service on AWS. Explored its capability to share file data across multiple compatible computing resources. Learned about common use cases involving applications that require a shared file system. 4. Knowledge of Amazon RDS Understood the fundamentals of relational databases and how data is organized into tables.
Learned about Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS) and its role in simplifying the deployment and management of relational databases on AWS.
Explored several database engines supported by Amazon RDS:
MySQL. PostgreSQL. MariaDB. Microsoft SQL Server. Oracle Database. Studied important Amazon RDS features:
Automated Backups: Automatically creates database backups according to the configured retention settings.
Multi-AZ Deployment: Improves database availability and supports recovery from infrastructure failures.
Read Replicas: Helps scale read workloads for supported database engines and configurations.
Monitoring: Provides metrics for observing database performance and operational health.
Recognized the importance of relational databases in applications that require structured data management and data consistency.
5. Knowledge of Amazon DynamoDB Learned that Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL database service provided by AWS.
Understood fundamental DynamoDB concepts:
Table: A collection of stored data items.
Item: An individual data record within a table.
Attribute: A data element describing an item.
Primary Key: A key used to uniquely identify each item within a table.
Explored the role of DynamoDB in applications requiring low latency and high scalability.
Understood the main differences between Amazon RDS and DynamoDB:
Amazon RDS: Suitable for relational data models and applications requiring SQL queries.
Amazon DynamoDB: Suitable for NoSQL applications requiring high scalability and fast access based on predefined query patterns.
6. Knowledge of Data Security and Backup Explored the importance of data security in cloud computing environments.
Studied fundamental data protection methods:
Encryption: Protects data during storage and transmission.
Access Control: Restricts access to authorized users and services.
Backup: Creates recoverable copies of data to support disaster recovery.
Versioning: Maintains historical versions of stored data to support recovery when necessary.
Understood the role of AWS IAM in controlling access to Storage and Database services.
Recognized the importance of choosing appropriate storage, backup, and recovery methods based on application requirements.
7. Comparison of AWS Storage and Database Services Service Service Type Primary Use Cases Amazon S3 Object Storage Storing images, videos, documents, backups, and unstructured data Amazon EBS Block Storage Providing persistent disk storage for Amazon EC2 Amazon EFS File Storage Providing shared file systems for compatible computing resources Amazon RDS Relational Database Managing relational data and SQL-based applications Amazon DynamoDB NoSQL Database Storing and retrieving NoSQL data with high scalability By comparing these services, I developed a better understanding of how different AWS storage and database solutions address different technical requirements.
Selecting an appropriate service depends on factors such as data structure, access patterns, performance, scalability, security, and operational costs.
8. Week 3 Summary During the third week of my internship, the main focus was on two important categories of Amazon Web Services: Storage and Database.
By studying Amazon S3, Amazon EBS, and Amazon EFS, I gained knowledge of common cloud storage models and how to select suitable storage solutions for different application requirements.
In addition, exploring Amazon RDS and Amazon DynamoDB helped me understand the differences between relational and non-relational databases, their fundamental characteristics, and their roles in modern application development.
The week also covered data protection principles, access management, and backup methods, emphasizing the importance of maintaining data security and system recoverability.
The knowledge acquired during Week 3 provides a foundation for exploring how applications are developed, deployed, and managed on AWS, particularly through Serverless services such as AWS Lambda, Amazon API Gateway, and Amazon CloudWatch in the following week.

title: Week 2 Worklog
content:
Objectives for Week 2 Understand the fundamental concepts of computer networking and the role of networking in Cloud Computing. Gain foundational knowledge of Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) and how networks are organized within AWS. Explore important VPC components, including Subnets, Route Tables, Internet Gateways, and Security Groups. Tasks to Be Completed This Week Day Tasks Start Date Completion Date References Monday - Study the fundamentals of Networking in Cloud Computing. - Research Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) and its role within AWS. - Learn about IP addresses, CIDR blocks, and basic network segmentation. - Compare traditional networking with cloud-based networking. 28/09/2026 28/09/2026 Amazon VPC Tuesday - Study Amazon VPC network architecture. - Learn about Public Subnets and Private Subnets. - Research Route Tables and traffic routing within a VPC. - Understand Internet Gateways and their role in connecting a VPC to the Internet. 29/09/2026 29/09/2026 Amazon VPC User Guide Wednesday - Explore network security mechanisms on AWS. - Study Security Groups and Network Access Control Lists (NACLs). - Compare Security Groups and NACLs. - Learn about Inbound Rules and Outbound Rules. - Research the principle of Least Privilege in system security. 30/09/2026 30/09/2026 VPC Security Thursday - Study AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). - Research IAM Users, Groups, Roles, and Policies. - Learn how to manage access permissions for AWS resources. - Understand the fundamentals of authentication and authorization in cloud environments. 01/10/2026 01/10/2026 AWS IAM Documentation Friday - Review Amazon VPC, Subnets, Route Tables, and Internet Gateways. - Practice designing a basic VPC network architecture diagram. - Explore the steps involved in configuring VPCs and Security Groups through the AWS Management Console. - Review and evaluate the components of the network architecture. - Summarize the knowledge gained during Week 2 and prepare to study AWS Storage & Database in Week 3. 02/10/2026 02/10/2026 AWS Workshops Achievements in Week 2 1. Knowledge of AWS Networking Understood the role of Networking in connecting and managing resources within a cloud computing environment. Gained a foundational understanding of Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) and its role in creating logically isolated virtual networks on AWS. Explored the fundamental components of computer networking: IP Address: An address used to identify devices and resources within a network. CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing): A method for representing and dividing IP address ranges. VPC: A logically isolated virtual network within the AWS environment. Subnet: A subdivision of an IP address range within a VPC. 2. Knowledge of Amazon VPC Architecture Explored the structure of Amazon VPC and how its networking components work together. Learned to distinguish between different subnet types: Public Subnet: A subnet with a route to an Internet Gateway, allowing appropriately configured resources to communicate directly with the Internet. Private Subnet: A subnet that does not have a direct route to an Internet Gateway. Understood the functions of important networking components: Route Table: Contains routing rules that determine how network traffic is directed. Internet Gateway: Enables communication between a VPC and the Internet when routing and security requirements are satisfied. Network Interface: A virtual networking component that connects resources to the network. 3. Knowledge of AWS Network Security Understood the role of Security Groups in controlling inbound and outbound traffic for AWS resources. Learned the differences between Security Groups and Network Access Control Lists: Security Group: Operates at the resource or network interface level and is stateful. Network ACL: Operates at the subnet level and is stateless. Distinguished between two types of traffic rules: Inbound Rules: Control incoming network traffic. Outbound Rules: Control outgoing network traffic. Recognized the importance of restricting network access and allowing only necessary connections. 4. Knowledge of AWS Identity and Access Management Understood the role of AWS IAM in managing identities and access permissions for AWS resources. Learned to distinguish between the main IAM components: IAM User: An identity created within an AWS account. IAM Group: A collection of IAM Users used to simplify permission management. IAM Role: An identity with a set of permissions that authorized entities can temporarily assume. IAM Policy: A document that defines access permissions for AWS resources. Understood the Principle of Least Privilege, which ensures that users and services receive only the permissions necessary to perform their tasks. Recognized the importance of Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) in strengthening account security. 5. Basic Network Architecture Design Practice Studied the process of building a simple Amazon VPC architecture. Designed a reference network diagram consisting of: One VPC with a defined CIDR block. One Public Subnet. One Private Subnet. One Internet Gateway. Route Tables for each subnet type. Security Groups to protect resources within the VPC. Understood the relationships between networking components when deploying applications on AWS. Became familiar with the procedures for configuring and inspecting networking resources through the AWS Management Console. 6. Week 2 Summary During the second week of the internship, the main focus was on two important areas of Amazon Web Services: Networking and Security.
By studying Amazon VPC, Subnets, Route Tables, Internet Gateways, Security Groups, and IAM, I developed a better understanding of how virtual networks are organized, how network connections are managed, and how access permissions are controlled within cloud environments.
In addition to theoretical knowledge, exploring the process of designing a basic network architecture helped me understand the relationships between networking components and the key considerations involved in developing secure cloud-based systems.
The knowledge acquired during Week 2 provides an important foundation for exploring AWS Storage and Database services, including Amazon S3, Amazon EBS, and Amazon RDS, in the following week.

title: Introduction
content:
VPC endpoints VPC endpoints are virtual devices. They are horizontally scaled, redundant, and highly available VPC components. They allow communication between your compute resources and AWS services without imposing availability risks. Compute resources running in VPC can access Amazon S3 using a Gateway endpoint. PrivateLink interface endpoints can be used by compute resources running in VPC or on-premises. Workshop overview In this workshop, you will use two VPCs.
“VPC Cloud” is for cloud resources such as a Gateway endpoint and an EC2 instance to test with. “VPC On-Prem” simulates an on-premises environment such as a factory or corporate datacenter. An EC2 instance running strongSwan VPN software has been deployed in “VPC On-prem” and automatically configured to establish a Site-to-Site VPN tunnel with AWS Transit Gateway. This VPN simulates connectivity from an on-premises location to the AWS cloud. To minimize costs, only one VPN instance is provisioned to support this workshop. When planning VPN connectivity for your production workloads, AWS recommends using multiple VPN devices for high availability.

title: Project Proposal
content:
Driver Drowsiness & Distraction Detection An Edge AI and AWS Serverless Solution for Driver-State Monitoring 1. Executive Summary Driver Drowsiness & Distraction Detection is a research and prototype-development project that combines Computer Vision, Edge AI, and AWS Cloud to identify observable signs potentially associated with driver drowsiness or distraction. The objective is to support earlier awareness of unusual driver behavior, not to replace certified vehicle-safety systems or determine a driver’s medical condition.
The system captures facial images through a webcam and processes the video locally on an Edge Device. Python, OpenCV, and MediaPipe Face Mesh (478 facial landmarks, as specified in the project proposal) support the extraction of Eye Aspect Ratio (EAR), Mouth Aspect Ratio (MAR), Head Pose, and an experimental Gaze Direction feature. Temporal Analysis, CSV-based examination, and rule-based candidates are used to investigate changes over time rather than relying on single-frame decisions.
The proposed cloud architecture sends event metadata only, not raw webcam video, to Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API). AWS Lambda validates the events and uses conditional writes to Amazon DynamoDB. Amazon Cognito provides dashboard authentication, while a private Amazon S3 origin and Amazon CloudFront are intended to deliver the web interface. Amazon CloudWatch, IAM, CloudTrail, and AWS Budgets support operations, security, and cost control; AWS WAF remains optional.
Current status: The Edge image-processing pipeline has been built and the AWS architecture has been designed. Local Event Buffer/Retry, temporal-analysis refinement, Gaze evaluation, cloud integration, and resilience testing remain to be completed or validated. The proposal describes the intended system, not a fully deployed production service.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? A driver may display signs such as prolonged eye closure, yawning, changes in head posture, or changes in gaze direction. Detecting and interpreting these signs consistently is challenging because facial behavior varies across people and depends on lighting, camera angle, occlusion, and motion.
A cloud-only design that continuously uploads video can create additional bandwidth usage, latency, operational costs, and privacy risks. A monitoring prototype should therefore distinguish local visual analysis from remote event storage, remain useful during connectivity interruptions, and avoid presenting uncertain observations as definitive diagnoses.
The Solution The project adopts a hybrid Edge AI + AWS Serverless architecture:
Local capture and analysis: The webcam supplies frames to OpenCV and MediaPipe. The Edge pipeline extracts EAR, MAR, Head Pose, and experimental Gaze features. Temporal assessment: CSV analysis and rule-based candidates examine patterns across time to identify events worth recording; thresholds and rules require evaluation. Local buffering: Each event is associated with an event_id. The planned Local Event Buffer retains metadata when the network is unavailable, while Retry attempts synchronization after connectivity returns. Cloud event ingestion: The Edge Device sends metadata via HTTPS POST to API Gateway. Lambda Event Writer validates the request and uses DynamoDB Conditional PutItem to help prevent duplicate writes by event_id. Protected history access: The dashboard uses Amazon Cognito and JWT authorization for its protected API routes. Lambda Event Reader queries DynamoDB and returns the permitted event history. Distribution and monitoring: CloudFront delivers the Frontend from a private S3 origin using Origin Access Control (OAC). CloudWatch provides operational logs and metrics. The design keeps video processing at the Edge. Its cloud component is intended to handle metadata, access, storage, and observability, rather than remote video inference.
Benefits and Practical Value Privacy-oriented design: Raw video is not transmitted to AWS in the proposed workflow. Reduced network dependence: Face and feature analysis can continue locally; synchronization is designed to resume after temporary network failures. Manageable infrastructure: API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB reduce the need to administer application servers. Reviewable events: The proposed dashboard allows authorized users to retrieve recorded event history. Learning outcomes: The project connects AI/Computer Vision development with AWS security, serverless services, frontend delivery, and monitoring. No measured improvement in crash rates, financial return, or operating-cost savings is claimed at this stage.
3. Solution Architecture The design consists of three logical layers: Edge Processing, AWS Event Backend, and Web Dashboard. Only event metadata crosses the Edge-to-Cloud boundary.
EDGE PROCESSING (local device) Webcam -> OpenCV -> MediaPipe Face Mesh (478 landmarks) -> EAR / MAR / Head Pose / experimental Gaze -> CSV Analysis + Temporal / Rule-based Candidates -> Event Metadata (event_id) -> Planned Local Event Buffer + Retry | HTTPS POST (metadata only) v AWS EVENT BACKEND Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) -> AWS Lambda Event Writer (validation) -> Amazon DynamoDB (Conditional PutItem by event_id) WEB DASHBOARD / HISTORY PATH Browser -> Amazon Cognito (sign-in / JWT) -> API Gateway (JWT Authorizer for protected routes) -> AWS Lambda Event Reader -> Amazon DynamoDB -> Event History -> Browser Frontend delivery: private Amazon S3 -> CloudFront (OAC) -> Browser Observability: CloudWatch | Access control: IAM | Audit: CloudTrail Cost management: AWS Budgets | Optional additional protection: AWS WAF Figure 1 – Proposed Edge AI and AWS Cloud architecture (text diagram). This is a design representation, not proof that the cloud components have been deployed.
AWS Services Used AWS Service Intended Responsibility Status in Source Proposal Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) Receive Edge event submissions and dashboard requests Architecture designed AWS Lambda – Event Writer Validate event metadata and write events Architecture designed Amazon DynamoDB Store event history and support conditional writes Architecture designed AWS Lambda – Event Reader Retrieve event history for the dashboard Architecture designed Amazon Cognito User registration, sign-in, and JWT issuance Architecture designed Amazon S3 Private hosting origin for frontend assets Architecture designed Amazon CloudFront + OAC Deliver the frontend while restricting direct S3 access Architecture designed Amazon CloudWatch API access logs, Lambda logs/errors/duration, DynamoDB metrics Monitoring design proposed AWS IAM Service permissions and least-privilege access Supporting control proposed AWS CloudTrail AWS account activity auditing Supporting control proposed AWS Budgets Budget monitoring and alerts Supporting control proposed AWS WAF Additional application-layer protection Optional Component Design Edge AI Processing
Input: Webcam video, processed locally with OpenCV. Facial analysis: MediaPipe Face Mesh provides 478 landmarks as described in the project source. Feature extraction: EAR, MAR, Head Pose, and experimental Gaze Direction. Temporal analysis: CSV analysis and rule-based candidates; the final algorithm still requires refinement and validation. Event synchronization: Proposed event_id, Local Event Buffer, and Retry handling; not yet confirmed as complete. Cloud Event Processing
Ingestion: API Gateway receives HTTPS POST event requests containing metadata rather than raw video. Validation and persistence: Lambda Event Writer validates data before DynamoDB conditional writes to help avoid duplicates. History retrieval: Protected dashboard requests reach Lambda Event Reader through API Gateway and are answered from DynamoDB. Frontend, Identity, and Operations
Authentication: Cognito issues JWTs for dashboard sign-in; API Gateway JWT Authorizer protects designated routes. Distribution: CloudFront serves static frontend files from a private S3 bucket through OAC. Operations: CloudWatch monitors service behavior; IAM, CloudTrail, and Budgets support access control, auditing, and cost awareness. Security design note: The source describes JWT authorization for dashboard access but does not specify the final authentication method for Edge ingestion. That control must be defined and tested before external deployment. JWT validation alone also does not establish per-user authorization of every DynamoDB item.
4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases The project is organized into the following work packages. Their sequence is a planning structure, not a claim that all phases have been completed.
Research and Edge proof of concept: Study drowsiness/distraction indicators, build webcam processing with OpenCV and MediaPipe, and extract EAR, MAR, Head Pose, and experimental Gaze features. Status: Edge pipeline built; Gaze still experimental. Temporal interpretation and evaluation: Use CSV-based analysis and rule-based candidates to study changes across frames, refine event criteria, and evaluate false warnings. Status: Initial approach established; further work required. Reliable local event handling: Define the event metadata contract and event_id, implement a Local Event Buffer, and verify retry/resynchronization after network interruption. Status: Designed; completion and failure testing pending. AWS backend and dashboard integration: Configure API Gateway, Lambda Writer/Reader, DynamoDB, Cognito, private S3/CloudFront OAC, and monitoring. Confirm permissions and end-to-end event history retrieval. Status: Cloud architecture designed; full deployment not verified by the source. Validation and documentation: Test varied lighting and camera angles, network outages, event duplication, backend failures, access control, monitoring, and budget alerts. Document actual findings and limitations. Status: Planned / requires evidence. Technical Requirements Edge equipment: A webcam and a computer capable of running the local Computer Vision pipeline. The source does not specify required CPU/GPU specifications. Edge software: Python, OpenCV, MediaPipe Face Mesh, temporal processing and CSV analysis, plus a planned local buffer and retry component. Cloud services: Amazon API Gateway, AWS Lambda, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon Cognito, Amazon S3, Amazon CloudFront, and Amazon CloudWatch; supporting IAM, CloudTrail, AWS Budgets, and optional WAF. Data contract: Metadata-only event submissions with a unique event_id; the final schema, retention period, and data access rules are to be finalized. Privacy and security: No raw video uploads, least-privilege service roles, authenticated dashboard requests, and explicit authorization of event-history access. Evaluation: Review event recognition quality, false alarms, latency, network resilience, and behavior in difficult visual conditions. Numerical targets are not yet established. 5. Timeline & Milestones The original project document does not specify confirmed calendar dates or completed milestones. The following is a proposed mapping to the FCAJ Week 6–12 worklog structure; it should be adjusted to match actual work records.
Proposed Period Focus Evidence / Deliverable Week 6 Problem research and requirements Problem definition, initial features, functional and privacy requirements Week 7 Architecture and data-flow design Edge–Cloud diagram, event flow, AWS service responsibilities Week 8 Core Edge functionality Webcam processing, feature extraction, initial temporal candidates Week 9 Integration and testing Local metadata flow, AWS integration checks, test records Week 10 Evaluation and optimization Lighting/angle testing, false-alert analysis, performance observations Week 11 Finalization and documentation Improved reliability, setup notes, architecture and test documentation Week 12 Final report and demonstration Verified outcomes, limitations, demonstration and internship report Milestone policy: Mark a milestone complete only after code, logs, screenshots, test records, or other supporting evidence confirms it. The source currently confirms an Edge pipeline and a designed Cloud architecture, not a completed end-to-end deployment.
6. Budget Estimation The project selects a serverless approach to limit fixed server-management overhead at an early stage. No actual AWS Pricing Calculator estimate or measured monthly AWS bill is included in the source proposal. Therefore, exact costs are intentionally left unreported rather than copied from the unrelated weather-platform template.
Infrastructure Cost Components Component Main Cost Driver to Estimate Amazon API Gateway Number of API requests AWS Lambda Requests, memory allocation, and execution duration Amazon DynamoDB Read/write activity and stored event data Amazon Cognito Applicable user/authentication pricing model Amazon S3 Frontend storage and requests Amazon CloudFront Data transfer and requests Amazon CloudWatch Logs, retention, metrics, and alarms AWS CloudTrail Applicable audit logging and storage configuration AWS WAF (optional) Usage-based protection charges if enabled Edge hardware / network Existing hardware availability, local electricity, and connectivity Estimate required before deployment: Define expected devices, events per device/day, API calls, metadata size, stored history, dashboard usage, AWS Region, and log retention; then calculate costs with the AWS Pricing Calculator.
Cost controls: Configure AWS Budgets and alerts, review CloudWatch log retention, minimize unnecessary requests, and send only required metadata. No ROI or break-even period is claimed without measured inputs.
7. Risk Assessment Preliminary Risk Matrix The classifications below are planning judgments, not measured occurrence probabilities.
Risk Potential Impact Planned Response Unreliable or missing Internet connection Event metadata may not reach AWS immediately Local Event Buffer, Retry, and recovery testing Poor lighting, camera angle, or facial occlusion Incorrect facial measurements or missed features Evaluate across varied conditions; allow uncertain/unknown states Inaccurate temporal rules or false warnings Incorrect driver-state alerts Refine rules using recorded tests and review false-alarm cases Experimental Gaze Direction Unreliable distraction indication Keep Gaze experimental until separately validated Duplicate event submissions Duplicate history records Unique event_id and DynamoDB conditional writes Unauthorized event-history access Privacy and security exposure Cognito/JWT plus data-level authorization and IAM review Cloud outage or service misconfiguration Event ingestion or dashboard interruption Retain pending events locally; monitor and test recovery Unexpected AWS cost Budget overrun Budgets alerts, usage monitoring, and usage-based estimation Mitigation Strategies Detection reliability: Evaluate against varied lighting conditions and camera angles; document failures and uncertainty. Network resilience: Preserve pending event metadata locally and test delivery after reconnection. Data integrity: Apply a consistent event identifier and conditional insertion to minimize duplicates. Privacy: Keep raw video at the Edge; restrict and audit access to stored metadata. Cloud observability: Review CloudWatch logs, error rates, execution duration, and DynamoDB activity. Cost governance: Use AWS Budgets and re-check estimates as traffic increases. Contingency Plans If the Internet is unavailable, continue local analysis and retain unsynchronized events until transfer is possible, subject to the buffer’s eventual tested behavior. If facial features are unreliable, avoid definitive interpretation and record the limitation for evaluation. If a cloud component fails, inspect logs and permissions, correct the issue, and retest before considering the integration complete. If costs increase unexpectedly, reduce nonessential usage and reconsider retention, logging, or optional services. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements Upon completion and validation, the system is expected to:
Process webcam video locally for facial feature extraction and temporal driver-state analysis. Identify potential drowsiness- or distraction-related events without uploading raw video to AWS. Create event metadata and synchronize it reliably through a buffer/retry mechanism. Store and retrieve event history using API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB. Provide a protected dashboard using Cognito, private S3 hosting, and CloudFront. Monitor service health and usage through CloudWatch and AWS Budgets. Long-term Value Demonstrate how Edge AI and AWS Serverless components can be combined in one application. Provide a modular foundation for improving temporal analysis and studying additional facial indicators. Support future evaluation of reliability, privacy, cost, and user experience. Serve as a technical learning outcome of the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) internship. Scope limitation: These are expected outcomes. Recognition accuracy, production readiness, and effectiveness in real driving conditions must be established through documented tests rather than assumed from the architecture alone.

Event Information Information Details Event Name AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026 – HCMC Watch Party Date September 29, 2026 Watch Party Location AWS Office, Ho Chi Minh City Main Event Venue JW Marriott Hotel Hanoi Organizer Amazon Web Services (AWS) Format Hybrid Watch Party and In-person Networking Topics Cloud Computing, Generative AI, Agentic AI, Modern Application Development 2. Purpose of the Event AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026 – HCMC Watch Party aimed to provide the technology community in Ho Chi Minh City with opportunities to explore emerging developments in Cloud Computing and Artificial Intelligence.
Through live broadcasts from the main event in Hanoi, participants could access technical presentations, learn about real-world cloud applications, and connect with local AWS community members.
The main objectives included:
Exploring Emerging Technologies: Understanding the latest developments in Cloud Computing, Generative AI, and Agentic AI. Expanding Technical Knowledge: Learning from AWS experts about modern application development and cloud architecture. Understanding Real-World AI Applications: Exploring how AI Agents support automation, task execution, and enterprise modernization. Discovering Cloud Solutions: Understanding the role of AWS services in building scalable applications. Building Professional Connections: Encouraging networking among developers, cloud engineers, and AI enthusiasts. Supporting Career Development: Identifying relevant technologies and professional skills in the Cloud and AI industries. 3. Main Activities and Event Highlights 3.1. Keynote – Cloud Computing and Agentic AI The program included keynote presentations broadcast from the main event in Hanoi.
These presentations explored how cloud technologies and artificial intelligence are helping organizations innovate, modernize applications, and develop new digital solutions.
Major topics included:
Emerging trends in Cloud Computing. The evolution from Generative AI to Agentic AI. AI Agents and workflow automation. Enterprise application modernization. Cloud scalability, security, and innovation. The main event featured Dr. Werner Vogels, CTO of Amazon, among its keynote speakers.
3.2. Builders x AI – Software Development with Agentic AI The Watch Party highlighted technical sessions from the Builders x AI track, focusing on modern approaches to software development.
Key technical concepts included:
Generative AI
Artificial intelligence systems capable of generating content such as text, software code, and other forms of data.
Agentic AI
An approach to developing AI systems that can plan tasks, interact with tools, and execute multi-step workflows.
AI-Assisted Software Development
The use of AI-powered tools to assist with programming, code analysis, testing, and software development processes.
Cloud-Native Applications
Applications designed to take advantage of the scalability, flexibility, and managed services available in cloud environments.
3.3. AI-Driven Application Modernization Another major theme of the main event was the application of Cloud Computing and AI to modernize enterprise technology systems.
The event program covered topics such as:
Cloud migration and infrastructure modernization. AI-assisted software engineering. Automated workflows powered by AI Agents. Building data foundations for AI applications. Improving operational efficiency and scalability. These topics highlighted the growing relationship between AI capabilities and cloud-based infrastructure.
3.4. AWS Community Networking in Ho Chi Minh City In addition to live-streamed presentations, the HCMC Watch Party provided opportunities for local technology professionals and enthusiasts to connect.
The networking component encouraged:
Sharing knowledge about AWS services. Discussing cloud development experiences. Exploring developments in Generative AI and Agentic AI. Building connections within the local developer community. 4. Knowledge and Insights Gained The event topics offered valuable perspectives on the development of AI-powered and cloud-native systems.
4.1. Understanding Agentic AI Agentic AI represents an important direction in artificial intelligence development.
By combining language models with external tools, APIs, and data sources, AI Agents can be designed to complete complex tasks through multiple steps.
This approach extends beyond traditional chatbot interactions and supports more sophisticated automation workflows.
4.2. Understanding the Role of Cloud Computing in AI Cloud Computing provides infrastructure and managed services that support the development, deployment, and operation of modern AI applications.
Cloud environments allow organizations to scale resources, manage data, and integrate multiple software components according to their needs.
4.3. Exploring Modern Software Development Artificial intelligence is increasingly being integrated into software development processes.
AI-powered development tools can assist programmers with code generation, analysis, and testing.
However, effective implementation also requires software engineering knowledge, system design skills, and careful quality evaluation.
4.4. Recognizing the Value of Technology Communities Community events such as AWS Watch Parties provide opportunities to learn about emerging technologies, exchange technical knowledge, and connect with experienced professionals.
They also encourage continuous learning and professional development.
5. Conclusion AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026 – HCMC Watch Party provided an opportunity for the technology community in Ho Chi Minh City to engage with current developments in Cloud Computing and Artificial Intelligence.
By combining live-streamed technical presentations from Hanoi with local networking activities, the program helped connect technical knowledge with real-world industry applications.
In particular, the discussions surrounding Agentic AI and modern software development demonstrated how artificial intelligence is influencing the design, development, and operation of software systems.
Overall, the event highlighted the importance of continuous learning, practical technical skills, and participation in professional technology communities.

title: Create an S3 Interface endpoint
content:
In this section you will create and test an S3 interface endpoint using the simulated on-premises environment deployed as part of this workshop.
Return to the Amazon VPC menu. In the navigation pane, choose Endpoints, then click Create Endpoint.
In Create endpoint console:
Name the interface endpoint In Service category, choose aws services In the Search box, type S3 and press Enter. Select the endpoint named com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3. Ensure that the Type column indicates Interface. For VPC, select VPC Cloud from the drop-down. Make sure to choose “VPC Cloud” and not “VPC On-prem”
Expand Additional settings and ensure that Enable DNS name is not selected (we will use this in the next part of the workshop) Select 2 subnets in the following AZs: us-east-1a and us-east-1b For Security group, choose SGforS3Endpoint: Keep the default policy - full access and click Create endpoint Congratulation on successfully creating S3 interface endpoint. In the next step, we will test the interface endpoint.

title: Test the Gateway Endpoint
content:
Create S3 bucket Navigate to S3 management console In the Bucket console, choose Create bucket In the Create bucket console Name the bucket: choose a name that hasn’t been given to any bucket globally (hint: lab number and your name) Leave other fields as they are (default) Scroll down and choose Create bucket Successfully create S3 bucket. Connect to EC2 with session manager For this workshop, you will use AWS Session Manager to access several EC2 instances. Session Manager is a fully managed AWS Systems Manager capability that allows you to manage your Amazon EC2 instances and on-premises virtual machines (VMs) through an interactive one-click browser-based shell. Session Manager provides secure and auditable instance management without the need to open inbound ports, maintain bastion hosts, or manage SSH keys.
First Cloud AI Journey Lab for indepth understanding of Session manager.
In the AWS Management Console, start typing Systems Manager in the quick search box and press Enter: From the Systems Manager menu, find Node Management in the left menu and click Session Manager: Click Start Session, and select the EC2 instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. This EC2 instance is already running in “VPC Cloud” and will be used to test connectivity to Amazon S3 through the Gateway endpoint you just created (s3-gwe).
Session Manager will open a new browser tab with a shell prompt: sh-4.2 $
You have successfully start a session - connect to the EC2 instance in VPC cloud. In the next step, we will create a S3 bucket and a file in it.
Create a file and upload to s3 bucket Change to the ssm-user’s home directory by typing cd ~ in the CLI Create a new file to use for testing with the command fallocate -l 1G testfile.xyz, which will create a file of 1GB size named “testfile.xyz”. Upload file to S3 bucket with command aws s3 cp testfile.xyz s3://your-bucket-name. Replace your-bucket-name with the name of S3 bucket that you created earlier. You have successfully uploaded the file to your S3 bucket. You can now terminate the session.
Check object in S3 bucket Navigate to S3 console. Click the name of your s3 bucket In the Bucket console, you will see the file you have uploaded to your S3 bucket Section summary Congratulation on completing access to S3 from VPC. In this section, you created a Gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to upload an object. The upload worked because the Gateway endpoint allowed communication to S3, without needing an Internet Gateway attached to “VPC Cloud”. This demonstrates the functionality of the Gateway endpoint as a secure path to S3 without traversing the Public Internet.
